summary: Defines GMPLS OSPF routing enhancements to advertise signal compatibility constraints in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks, where not all optical signals work with all network elements.

eli5.summary: Some light signals only fit certain equipment. This lets the network tell everyone which fits where.

questions: how does ospf advertise wson signal compatibility
what is the optical node property tlv
how does ospf advertise optical signal compatibility
subtitle: How OSPF tells optical path computation which signals each piece of equipment can handle.

tldr.problem: In a Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON), not every optical signal is compatible with every network element, so path computation needs to know the signal compatibility limits of each node.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an Optical Node Property TLV with five sub-TLVs to the OSPF Traffic Engineering LSA, and defines a new WSON-LSC switching capability value (151) for interface descriptors.
tldr.outcome: Routers can flood WSON resource and compatibility information in OSPF. The detailed encodings live in RFC 7581, and this RFC is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7688 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The encodings it points to are defined in RFC 7581.

sections.title: The Compatibility Problem
sections.content:
In a Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON), not all the optical signals in the network are compatible with all the network elements taking part in it. Systems such as optical-electronic-optical (OEO) switches, regenerators and wavelength converters can be limited to processing only certain types of WSON signals. Signal compatibility is therefore an important constraint when computing a path.

RFC 7688 provides the GMPLS OSPF routing enhancements needed to advertise these constraints. The earlier documents RFC 6163, RFC 7446 and RFC 7581 explain how to extend the WSON control plane. A related document, RFC 7580, covers the more general routing and label assignment enhancements that apply beyond WSON.
sections.eli5: Imagine a toy train set where some tracks only fit some trains. Before planning a trip, you need to know which tracks fit your train. This RFC is how the network shares that information.

sections.title: The Optical Node Property TLV
sections.content:
RFC 3630 defines the OSPF Traffic Engineering (TE) Link State Advertisement (LSA) as an opaque LSA. RFC 7688 adds one new top-level TLV for use in it: the Optical Node Property TLV. It describes a single node and is made of optional sub-TLVs, with no ordering requirements between them.

At least one Optical Node Property TLV MUST be advertised in each LSA. More than one MAY be advertised in a single LSA to allow fine-grained topology changes, and implementations MUST support receiving several of them in one LSA. The detailed encodings of the properties are defined in RFC 7581.

Each sub-TLV may occur at most once in a given Optical Node TLV under one TE LSA. If a duplicate arrives in the same LSA, the redundant one SHOULD be ignored. If the same sub-TLV shows up in a different TE LSA, which would only happen through a packaging error, the one with the largest LSA ID SHOULD be picked. Unrecognized sub-TLVs are ignored.
sections.eli5: Each machine fills out one information card about itself. The card has up to five labeled boxes, and anyone reading it just skips boxes they do not understand.

sections.title: The Five Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Five sub-TLV types are defined, all of variable length:

  • Resource Block Information (1): the signal constraints and processing capabilities of a node, as defined in RFC 7446.
  • Resource Accessibility (2): how the resource pool relates to the switching device, meaning whether an ingress port can reach a resource block and whether a block can reach a given egress port.
  • Resource Wavelength Constraints (3): resources such as wavelength converters may have limited input or output wavelength ranges, and not every wavelength can reach or leave every resource.
  • Resource Block Pool State (4): whether a single resource is available or in use, as a list of integers or a bitmap.
  • Resource Block Shared Access Wavelength Availability (5): wavelength availability on shared fibers, needed when resource blocks are reached over a shared fiber.

The Pool State and Shared Access sub-TLVs are dynamic, because they can change when a connection is set up or torn down. The other three are static. The dynamic ones can therefore be advertised in separate TE LSAs per OSPF router.
sections.eli5: The five boxes say what a machine can do, which doors lead to it, which colors of light it accepts, which parts are busy right now, and which shared pipes are free. Only the busy and free boxes change often.

sections.title: The WSON-LSC Switching Capability
sections.content:
The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor (ISCD) describes the switching capability of an interface, as in RFC 4202. RFC 7688 defines a new Switching Capability value for WSON: 151, named WSON-LSC. It MUST be used with Encoding Type Lambda, as defined in RFC 3471. With those values, the ISCD MUST be interpreted as in RFC 4203, with the optional inclusion of one or more Switching Capability Specific Information (SCSI) sub-TLVs.

Two types of Bandwidth sub-TLV may appear in the SCSI, in any order and in any number: Type 1, Available Labels, and Type 2, Shared Backup Labels. Both are defined in RFC 7579. Duplicated labels are ignored, and the label format of RFC 6205 MUST be used when advertising interfaces with the WSON-LSC switching capability.
sections.eli5: Each connection port gets a new type sticker saying it handles colors of light. Next to it can be lists of colors that are free and colors set aside as spares.

sections.title: Scalability, Timeliness and Errors
sections.content:
The RFC addresses the worry that LSAs could exceed the IP MTU. In a typical node configuration, meaning several hundred channels with an OEO element, the Optical Node Property TLV would be under 350 bytes. In the rare case that it does exceed the MTU, IP fragmentation and reassembly is an acceptable method. If the LSA is too large, the sub-TLVs can also be packed into separate LSAs.

Synchronization is simple from the viewpoint of path computation. Until a Resource Block Information sub-TLV has been received for a system, path computation cannot use the other four, because it does not know what kind of resources they describe. Once it arrives, path computation can proceed with whatever other sub-TLVs it has. Out-of-date or missing information can lead either to a computed path that does not exist or to failing to find a path that does.

If the new sub-TLVs or their encodings are malformed, an implementation SHOULD log the problem and MUST stop sending the LSA that contains them. Implementations MUST rate-limit such logs, and the rate limit SHOULD be configurable. The signaling or management mechanism that sets up the connection is ultimately responsible for ensuring signal compatibility.
sections.eli5: The info cards are small, so they normally fit in one envelope. If you are missing the first card describing what the machine is, the other cards are not useful yet, so route planners wait for it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Actions
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no security issues beyond those in RFC 3630 and RFC 4203. The extensions live in Opaque LSAs, which are not used for Shortest Path First computation or normal routing, so they have no direct effect on IP routing. Tampering with GMPLS TE LSAs may, however, affect the underlying transport. The mechanisms of RFC 2328 apply to Opaque LSAs in OSPFv2, and RFC 5920 covers GMPLS security in general.

IANA registered the Optical Node Property top-level TLV as value 6 and created a registry for its sub-TLVs, where values 1 to 5 are assigned and 6 to 65535 are unassigned. It also registered switching type 151 (WSON-LSC) and created a registry for WSON-LSC SCSI sub-TLVs, with 1 for Available Labels and 2 for Shared Backup Labels. Both new registries use Standards Action.
sections.eli5: The new messages are only notes passed between routers, so they do not change normal routing. Still, someone who fakes them could confuse the optical equipment, so the old safety rules still apply.
